state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it like this: if you have a group of friends and you all grow by 3 cm, would everyone still be in the same order from shortest to tallest? Think about how that relates to the range of the plant heights.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Yeah, I guess everyone would still be in the same order... so like, if the shortest plant is still the shortest and the tallest is still the tallest, then the difference between them would be the same? But wait, I'm confused because I thought adding the same amount to everything wouldn't change the range, so why did I say only Tom was right?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think back to the misconception about a lower average meaning the data is more consistent. Just like how a lower average doesn't necessarily mean the data is more consistent, adding the same amount to every plant may not necessarily keep the range the same. Let's explore this idea further together.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher introduces an irrelevant misconception about averages in Turn 3, provides mathematically incorrect guidance suggesting adding a constant might change the range, and fails to help the student recognize that Katie (not Tom) is correct, leaving the student more confused than at the start.
score.justification_pass2: While Turn 1 uses a concrete analogy about friends growing taller, Turn 3 abandons the experiential approach entirely by referencing an unrelated abstract misconception about averages rather than continuing with real-world grounding.
